title: Bounded Streaming Frequency Index
summary: Design an in-memory index that answers frequency queries over a moving event window while controlling memory growth.
prompt: Design the algorithm and interfaces for a service component that receives timestamped string keys and answers how many times a key appeared during the most recent W seconds. Events arrive in timestamp order. Explain the data structures, update and query operations, cleanup strategy, and tests you would use before implementation.
context: A telemetry pipeline emits up to 20,000 events per second.
The window W is configured once when the component starts and may be as large as one hour.
Most keys are short strings, but the number of distinct keys is not known in advance.
deliverables: A precise interface for recording events and querying a key.
The core algorithm and supporting data structures.
Time and space complexity for updates, queries, and cleanup.
Edge cases involving window boundaries, idle keys, and bursts.
A focused test plan with representative sequences.
constraints: Use process memory only; persistence is outside this exercise.
Do not assume a fixed key vocabulary.
A query at time T counts events with timestamps in the interval (T - W, T].
Favor correctness and bounded cleanup work over clever compression.
success_criteria: Window-boundary semantics are unambiguous.
Expired data can be reclaimed without scanning every known key per event.
Complexity claims match the proposed operations.
Tests demonstrate empty, boundary, burst, and long-idle behavior.
workflow: Write the time-window invariant in one sentence.
Sketch the update and query interfaces.
Choose a representation and trace a small event sequence.
Analyze cleanup cost and memory growth.
Write boundary-focused tests before refining the explanation.

guidance.title: One direction to explore
considerations: Consider whether exact per-event timestamps are necessary or whether fixed-duration buckets preserve the required semantics.
Separate the global expiry order from per-key counts so cleanup does not scan inactive keys.
Test the exact instant an event leaves the open-left window boundary.

common_mistakes: Keeping every event forever and calling cleanup an implementation detail.
Using a full-key scan on every record operation.
Leaving the inclusive and exclusive window boundaries undefined.
Claiming constant memory without relating it to event rate and window length.
stretch_goals: Discuss out-of-order events with bounded lateness.
Explore approximate counting when exact memory cost is too high.

title: Overlap-Aware Capacity Planner
summary: Compute whether scheduled workloads exceed a shared capacity and return the first violating time range with useful evidence.
prompt: Given half-open workload intervals [start, end) with positive capacity demands and a fixed system capacity, design an algorithm that reports every maximal time range where total demand exceeds capacity. For each range, include the peak demand and the workload IDs active at the first violation point.
context: Times are integer minutes but may be large and sparse.
Up to 200,000 workload intervals may be supplied in one planning run.
Several intervals can start or end at the same minute.
deliverables: An algorithm with clearly defined event ordering.
Complexity analysis in terms of workloads and returned violations.
Handling of ties, zero-length input, and touching intervals.
Implementation considerations for tracking active IDs.
Test cases covering nested, disjoint, and simultaneous intervals.
constraints: Intervals use half-open semantics.
A workload ID is unique within an input set.
Do not iterate across every minute in the time domain.
Output ranges must be maximal and sorted.
success_criteria: Start/end tie ordering preserves half-open semantics.
The algorithm scales with input size rather than coordinate range.
Returned ranges merge continuous violation periods correctly.
Active-ID evidence is accurate at the first violating point.
workflow: Define interval and violation semantics.
Transform a small example into ordered events.
Decide how demand and active IDs change at a shared timestamp.
Derive output-range construction and complexity.
Attack the design with ties and nested intervals.

guidance.title: Questions to test
considerations: A sweep-line representation can avoid dependence on the size of the time coordinate.
At the same timestamp, applying ending events before starting events can encode half-open intervals.
Consider the cost of copying active IDs and whether evidence is needed only when a violation begins.

common_mistakes: Iterating minute by minute.
Processing starts before ends at a shared boundary.
Returning fragmented ranges for one continuous violation.
Ignoring the output cost of materializing active IDs.
stretch_goals: Support incremental insertion and removal of workloads.
Return the minimal set of workloads whose removal restores capacity.

title: Multi-Region Feature Flag Control Plane
summary: Design a control plane and read path that distribute flag changes globally without making application requests depend on a central service.
prompt: Design a multi-region feature flag platform for internal services. Operators create versioned rules, applications evaluate flags locally, and emergency disables should propagate quickly. Produce an architecture that makes consistency, safety, rollback, tenancy, and regional failure behavior explicit.
context: The platform serves 15 regions and thousands of application instances.
Read availability matters more than immediate global consistency for ordinary changes.
Emergency disable operations have a stricter propagation objective than routine edits.
deliverables: Rule/version data model and distribution events.
constraints: Application evaluation must not require a network call on every request.
Rules must be auditable and tenant-isolated.
A bad rule must be recoverable without editing it in place.
Regional disconnection must have an explicit behavior.
success_criteria: Control and evaluation paths are separated.
Versioning and rollback behavior are concrete.
Propagation and stale-read risks are observable.
The design states how it behaves during regional and distribution failures.
workflow: Define ordinary and emergency change objectives.
Separate operator writes from application evaluation.
Model immutable versions and activation state.
Trace rollout, rollback, and regional partition scenarios.
Add observability and operational controls.

guidance.title: One direction to explore
considerations: Treat published rule versions as immutable artifacts and activation as a separate decision.
Compare streaming distribution with periodic snapshot recovery.
Ask which component can safely initiate an emergency disable when the primary control region is unavailable.

common_mistakes: Putting a synchronous central lookup on the request path.
Treating propagation delay as invisible.
Overwriting rules without an audit or rollback model.
Ignoring how SDKs recover after missing distribution events.
stretch_goals: Design staged percentage rollout with deterministic assignment.
Add rule simulation against recorded, privacy-safe attributes.

title: Durable Webhook Delivery Platform
summary: Design reliable customer webhook delivery with retries, ordering choices, replay controls, and protection against unhealthy destinations.
prompt: Design a platform that accepts internal domain events and delivers signed webhooks to customer endpoints. Customers need delivery history and controlled replay. Explain delivery guarantees, retry scheduling, endpoint isolation, security, and operational recovery.
context: Peak intake is 50,000 events per second across many tenants.
Destination latency and availability are outside your control.
Some event types require per-resource ordering while others do not.
deliverables: Subscription, attempt, and replay data model.
External management APIs and internal events.
Retry, backpressure, and endpoint isolation strategy.
constraints: Delivery is at least once; consumers may receive duplicates.
Payload signatures must support key rotation.
One unhealthy tenant endpoint must not block unrelated tenants.
Replay must be bounded and auditable.
success_criteria: Durability boundaries and state transitions are clear.
Duplicate delivery and ordering are handled explicitly.
Retry storms and toxic endpoints are contained.
Operators can understand and safely replay failed deliveries.
workflow: Choose delivery and ordering semantics.
Model one event through every durable state.
Design partitioning and retry scheduling.
Trace slow, failing, and malicious endpoints.
Add customer and operator observability.

guidance.title: Considerations
considerations: Separate immutable event payloads from mutable delivery attempts.
Use explicit idempotency identifiers even though the receiver controls its own deduplication.
Consider per-endpoint circuit breaking and fair scheduling across tenants.

common_mistakes: Promising exactly-once delivery over HTTP.
Retrying every failure immediately.
Conflating event creation with delivery attempt state.
Providing unrestricted replay without audit or rate control.
stretch_goals: Support payload transformation with safe versioning.
Design regional failover without reordering every stream.

title: Support Ticket Routing with Abstention
summary: Design an ML-assisted router that assigns support queues when confident and safely abstains when it is not.
prompt: Design an ML system that recommends a support queue for each incoming ticket while preserving a manual triage path. The system should optimize time to appropriate ownership without silently misrouting rare or high-risk requests.
context: Tickets contain text, product metadata, locale, and customer tier.
Queue definitions and ownership change over time.
Historical assignments include transfers and inconsistent agent behavior.
deliverables: Problem framing, prediction target, and abstention policy.
constraints: Manual triage must remain available.
Sensitive ticket text needs access controls and retention limits.
The model must handle new queues and changing taxonomy.
A recommendation is not an automatic resolution decision.
success_criteria: Labels account for transfers and noisy historical choices.
Abstention and human review are first-class behavior.
Metrics distinguish routing speed from routing correctness.
Drift, taxonomy change, and subgroup failures are monitored.
workflow: Define the decision and the cost of each error.
Create a label policy from noisy assignment history.
Set a baseline and abstention threshold strategy.
Design online serving and manual fallback.
Close the loop with delayed outcome and drift monitoring.

guidance.title: Questions to test
considerations: The first assigned queue may not be the best label when a ticket is transferred.
A rules or retrieval baseline can expose whether a learned model adds value.
Confidence calibration matters when the product action includes abstention.

common_mistakes: Optimizing only top-one accuracy.
Training directly on every historical assignment.
Forcing a model prediction for every ticket.
Ignoring queue taxonomy changes and new-product cold starts.
stretch_goals: Recommend both queue and required specialist skill.
Design an active-learning queue for high-value uncertain examples.

title: Near-Duplicate Knowledge Base Detector
summary: Design a retrieval and review system that finds semantically overlapping documents without collapsing legitimately distinct guidance.
prompt: Design a system that identifies likely duplicate or substantially overlapping knowledge-base articles across multiple business units. It should generate review candidates, explain why a pair was surfaced, and learn from reviewer decisions without automatically deleting content.
context: The corpus contains millions of documents in multiple languages.
Exact duplicates are easy; partial and semantic overlap creates the real workload.
Permissions differ by business unit and must apply during retrieval and review.
deliverables: Product decision, candidate definition, and human review path.
Candidate generation, features, and model stages.
constraints: The system may recommend review but cannot delete or merge content.
Unauthorized document content must not leak through candidates or explanations.
New and edited documents should become searchable within an hour.
Multilingual behavior must be measured rather than assumed.
success_criteria: Candidate generation and final ranking are separated.
Permission filtering is enforced before exposure.
Evaluation reflects reviewer utility and false-positive cost.
Index freshness, representation drift, and language performance are observable.
workflow: Define duplicate categories and reviewer action.
Build a judged evaluation set with hard negatives.
Choose candidate generators and ranking signals.
Design permission-aware indexing and explanations.
Trace feedback, freshness, and model migration.

guidance.title: One direction to explore
considerations: Combine high-recall lexical and embedding retrieval before a more expensive pairwise ranker.
Use section-level evidence to make reviewer explanations concrete.
Treat permissions as retrieval constraints, not a UI-only filter.

common_mistakes: Using one similarity threshold as the entire system.
Evaluating only on easy exact duplicates.
Leaking titles or snippets across permission boundaries.
Treating reviewer disagreement as simple label noise.
stretch_goals: Suggest a canonical article without making the merge decision.
Support a staged embedding-model index migration.

title: Idempotent Background Job Processor
summary: Specify a job processor that survives retries, worker crashes, and duplicate delivery without performing external effects twice.
prompt: Design the interfaces and persistent state for a background job processor that charges an external API and records the result. Queue delivery is at least once, workers may crash at any point, and the external API supports caller-provided idempotency keys.
context: Jobs can be retried automatically or replayed manually by an operator.
The queue visibility timeout can expire while a slow worker is still running.
Operators need to distinguish pending, running, succeeded, retryable, and terminal work.
deliverables: Persistent job and attempt data model.
Retry, dead-letter, and operator recovery behavior.
constraints: Assume at-least-once queue delivery.
Do not rely on a distributed transaction with the external API.
Manual replay must preserve an audit trail.
Two workers may receive the same job concurrently.
success_criteria: External idempotency and internal state transitions reinforce each other.
Concurrency control is explicit.
Crash points are traced before and after the external call.
Tests include duplicate delivery, lease expiry, and ambiguous responses.
workflow: List every crash boundary.
Define job and attempt states.
Choose claim/lease and concurrency semantics.
Connect stable idempotency keys to the external call.
Design recovery, tests, metrics, and operator tools.

guidance.title: Failure modes to explore
considerations: Trace a crash after the external effect succeeds but before local success is recorded.
Keep the logical job identity separate from individual delivery attempts.
Consider compare-and-set state transitions or leases with fencing behavior.

common_mistakes: Assuming queue acknowledgement makes the external effect exactly once.
Generating a new idempotency key for every retry.
Using a lease without handling a stale worker.
Discarding attempt history when an operator replays work.
stretch_goals: Support fair scheduling and per-tenant concurrency limits.

title: API Usage Budget Service
summary: Design a low-latency service that enforces tenant usage budgets across regions while remaining operable during partial failure.
prompt: Design the API, data model, and consistency strategy for a service that decides whether a tenant may consume a requested number of API units. Budgets reset on defined calendar boundaries, traffic is multi-region, and downstream services need a fast allow-or-deny decision.
context: A request may consume more than one unit.
Some products require strict hard limits; others permit a small documented overshoot.
Billing records are authoritative later, but request-time enforcement cannot wait for billing aggregation.
deliverables: Budget, reservation, and ledger data model.
constraints: The hot decision path targets low double-digit millisecond latency.
Retries must not consume the same logical request twice.
The design must state whether and where overshoot is possible.
Reset boundaries use an explicit configured timezone.
success_criteria: Strict and tolerant enforcement modes are distinguished.
Idempotency and concurrent reservations are concrete.
Regional failure behavior matches the stated overshoot policy.
Ledger reconciliation can detect and explain divergence.
workflow: Define strictness and overshoot policy.
Write the request and idempotency contract.
Model reservations, consumption, expiry, and reset.
Compare coordination and regional-allocation strategies.
Trace retry, partition, clock, and reconciliation scenarios.

guidance.title: Tradeoffs to test
considerations: Compare a globally coordinated counter with preallocated regional budget slices.
A reservation lifecycle can separate authorization from final consumption.
Use stable request identity and a ledger to make reconciliation explainable.

common_mistakes: Claiming strict global enforcement with independent regional counters.
Leaving reservation expiry undefined.
Using wall-clock reset logic without timezone and boundary tests.
Treating the cache as both the authority and the audit ledger.
stretch_goals: Support hierarchical organization and project budgets.
Add soft warnings before a hard enforcement threshold.
